## The people of the land

**People of the land (decided 21 October 2026).** Each province's people are counted in three groups, one number each:

- **Settled:** the people on the land. They bring in the yield. Among them the men of fighting age are a number of their own, and every use of men draws on them: levies, police, builders whether paid or levied, porters, couriers and crews. Taking them hurts the harvest more than their share of the people, and how much follows the season: most at sowing and harvest, least in the slack months, which is when Egypt built, during the flood ("Seasons"). That is the only split by age or sex the game needs, since it is the one that changes decisions, and boys coming of age already carry a lost generation ("Births").
- **Under arms:** levied men away from their fields: soldiers in an army, porters, guards and couriers in caravans and the realm's courier service, and workers levied for building, the corvée (decided 21 October 2026). Each unit remembers the province it was drawn from, and its men go home there when it is disbanded.
- **Loose:** the landless, such as runaways, deserters, the displaced and the poor. They form bands, and loose men nobody has gathered are the province's banditry ("Pirates and bandits").

How the groups change:

- **Levying** moves settled people under arms, and the province's yield falls while they are away, so a long war costs harvests. Disbanding sends them home.
- **Battle counts its dead and its runaways.** A unit that loses a battle loses men: some die, which takes them from their home province and its men of fighting age for good, and some run, becoming loose men where the battle was lost. From item 13, a unit that falls back loses fewer than a destroyed one ("Battles: one season, losses, no dice"), and the winner loses some too. Sieges and storming kill townspeople as well as soldiers.
- **Famine, plague and war** kill settled people or push them off the land.
- **Peace, good harvests, investment and policing** bring loose men back to the land, or suppress them.
- **Births** let a province grow back slowly towards what its land can carry, so a ravaged province recovers over years, not seasons. Boys coming of age restore the men of fighting age more slowly still, over about a generation, so a great war leaves a lost generation for the rest of most games.
- **Recruiting** a band, or hiring mercenaries, draws on the loose.

**Where people go.**

- **Disbanding takes time.** Disbanded men walk home along the route like any traveller (build order item 7), and bring in no harvest until they arrive. Where a king disbands is his choice. At home, the men are soon back in the fields. Far away, some never arrive: discharged men far from home turn loose there, so an army disbanded abroad seeds banditry where it stood. Or he settles them in a province of his own that has room, as military colonists, and they become its settled people.
- **Settled people move within their kingdom.** Each season a small flow moves settled people between neighbouring provinces of the same kingdom, from the one more crowded for the food it has to the one with more room, in proportion to the difference, so it evens things out without swinging back and forth. Room is measured in food, the land's capacity plus the grain in store ("Feeding a province draws its people"). A ravaged province is refilled by its neighbours as well as by births, and conquered, emptied land fills slowly from the conqueror's core when it is joined to it, alongside the slow absorption of its yield (build order item 5).
- **Across borders, people flee.** Settled people leave their kingdom from famine, plague or war, as refugees, and, since taxes are now set by the king ("How a king lives"), from crushing taxes or hunger short of famine, as runaways (widened 21 October 2026); either way they arrive on the other side as loose men, so a greedy king loses people to his neighbours. There is no steady drift of farmers between kingdoms: kings held on to their people, and a constant pull across borders would wear away the differences between kingdoms and blur what a border means. Fugitives were common enough that treaties regulated them: Hittite treaties carry clauses for returning runaways, and the Amarna vassals complain of people going over to the Habiru.
- **Welcoming newcomers is a choice (decided 21 October 2026).** A king may settle refugees and loose men in a province of his with room, where they become its settled people, as Egypt let drought-stricken nomads into the Delta. It grows his land, but newcomers can stir unrest, and the king they fled may take it ill.
- **Fugitive clauses (decided 21 October 2026).** A tablet may promise to return runaways, and returning them is deportation in reverse ("Deportation"). Whether a king hands back a rival's runaways or keeps them as new hands for his fields is his choice, the one the treaties of the age wrote down.
- **The loose move freely.** They cross borders too, drifting towards wealth, bands and cities and away from policing, so banditry wanders towards rich and weakly guarded neighbours, as the vassal letters complain.
- **Deportation (decided 21 October 2026).** The largest movements of people in this age were forced. A conqueror may move settled people from a province he has taken to one of his own, where they become its settled people. It strips the conquered land of yield and levies, fills his own, and stirs unrest in both, among the deported and among those left behind; their share of the purse goes with them only if he lets them carry it. Hittite kings deported conquered peoples by the thousand, Mursili II claiming tens of thousands from Arzawa, and Egypt brought captives home from its campaigns as labour. Deportees walk the route like any company, so they can die, flee or be freed on the way. Built with people of the land in item 10+.

All of these are flows between neighbouring provinces once a season, or travel along routes the engine already runs, so they are cheap and stay seeded and deterministic.

What follows: strength counts the yield as it is, so a ravaged province is worth less, and a conqueror who burns what he takes gains little; the true cost of a war shows in the fields; and bands and banditry are the same people, gathered or not. First guesses are tuned in item 18. The script kings must weigh it ("Every feature is every seat's"): a levy now is a smaller harvest later.

**People are worth having, not free to keep (decided 21 October 2026).** People are labour, soldiers and taxes, but they carry costs the game already counts: they eat, so beyond what the land carries every extra mouth is fed from stores or imports ("Feeding a province draws its people"); conquered peoples can rise ("Revolt follows conditions, not dice"); and loose men turn to banditry and rob the purse ("Bandits rob the purse"). So no king drives people away in ordinary times; he loses them only through his trade-offs, a tax too heavy, a levy too large, a famine left unanswered. But there are moments when he would be rid of some:

- breaking a rebellious province by deporting its people, as the Hittites and later the Assyrians did ("Deportation");
- a scorched frontier, a border province emptied so an invader finds nothing to eat;
- policing that pushes loose men onto weaker neighbours, the export of banditry the vassal letters accuse each other of;
- putting out of a besieged city the mouths that cannot fight, so its food lasts longer: an order for the besieged king, whose expelled become refugees outside the walls.

The balance is right when losing people hurts and moving them is a real choice.
